newsitem.title: CONGO: Last aid workers flee fighting in Congo capital.
newsitem.headline: Last aid workers flee fighting in Congo capital.

text.p: The last foreign aid workers pulled out of Congo's capital Brazzaville on Thursday, their work paralysed by a merciless battle for the airport that went on into the night.
"They have all left," international Red Cross (ICRC) spokesman Paolo dell'Oca said in the twin city of Kinshasa in former Zaire.
The handful of Red Cross workers, the last operating in the former French colonial capital, crossed the Congo river to Kinshasa by speedboat and canoe.
Dell'Oca said some 17,000 people had fled Brazzaville's inner suburbs for the edges of town to escape the shelling.
The city they left behind was plunged deeper into chaos as the battle for the prize of Maya-Maya airport, the heaviest since fighting began on June 5, raged on.

An estimated 1,000-3,000 have already died in the clashes between the forces of President Pascal Lissouba, a former plant geneticist, and his enemy Denis Sassou Nguesso, Congo's Marxist leader for 13 years.
The two were rivals for presidential elections next month.

The Bacongo suburb, once a haven of peace held by neutral city mayor Bernard Kolelas, has been hit by dozens of shells. Several landed in the maternity ward of a hospital on Wednesday, killing a woman who was giving birth.
"We don't know how many wounded there are. The staff, the patients, everyone fled," hospital spokesman Faustin Missakila said, standing amid the shattered buildings.
"This is a hospital, and in a neutral area."
Despite the shelling, Kolelas hosted fresh mediation talks with military leaders from both sides on Thursday. There was no clear progress.

A week-long ceasefire he brokered took some sting out of the battles and let 1,250 French soldiers leave peacefully after evacuating foreigners, but it collapsed when Sassou launched his assault for the airport on Wednesday.
Both sides trumpeted victory while the shells rained down.
The fresh fighting dashed hopes of a swift deployment of a planned U.N. peacekeeping force, whose arrival was made dependent on a firm truce and a demilitarised airport.

Losing Maya-Maya, about five km (three miles) from the dissected city centre, would be a big blow to Lissouba, but Kinshasa pilots who spoke to Brazzaville control tower by radio said they were told his forces were still in place.
"There was an incursion yesterday but it was repulsed and Sassou's bandits abandoned a tank with some dead in it," a Lissouba spokesman said.
"Maya-Maya has been under the control of General Sassou's partisans since yesterday afternoon," an aide to Sassou said in his northern suburbs stronghold. "We're at war."

Paris, which says it will not send soldiers for an intervention force, protested after panicky government troops assaulted its ambassador Raymond Cesaire, beat up his bodyguard and shot at escorts as they left Lissouba's palace after talks.
Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left, said he would carry on working from his embassy, 200 metres (yards) from the front line.
